evals.prompt: How does your 5-runtime scoring model evaluate an interactive agent with `30-minute` sessions, moderate non-GPU CPU/RAM, heavy I/O wait on LLM calls, and MCP tool usage across `agentcore`, `ecs`, `eks`, `lambda`, and `lambda_microvms` when no live `current-run-verifications.json` check has been run yet?
evals.expected_output: Evaluates all 5 GA runtimes (`agentcore`, `ecs`, `eks`, `lambda`, `lambda_microvms`) across the 15 scoring dimensions (`NEUTRAL_SCORE = 2`), surfaces any runtime within `TIE_THRESHOLD = 2` points of the top score as `co_recommend`, explains that without `current-run-verifications.json` (`verification_required` constraints such as `lambda` `15m` timeout and `lambda_microvms.*` capabilities) are **deferred rather than hard-eliminated** so `recommendation_status` is marked **`provisional`**, and warns never to fabricate or embed verification records inside `seed.json` or `answers.json`.
expectations: Activates the agent-advisor skill
Evaluates all 5 GA runtimes (`agentcore`, `ecs`, `eks`, `lambda`, `lambda_microvms`) including the `TIE_THRESHOLD = 2` co-recommendation rule

Explains that unverified `verification_required` constraints (`lambda` 15m timeout, `lambda_microvms`) are deferred rather than hard-eliminated without `current-run-verifications.json` (yielding `provisional` status)

evals.prompt: Compare AgentCore compute type and deployment pattern selection for two workloads: (A) a single-agent Strands assistant with `45-minute` sessions, `2 vCPU / 4 GB RAM`, no GPU, spending 80% of time waiting on LLM/API I/O; and (B) a `12-hour` multi-agent CrewAI code-migration system needing `32 GB RAM` and specific EC2 instance families.
evals.expected_output: Routes Workload A to `agentcore_compute_type = "microvms"` (`<= 8h` max session, `<= 2 vCPU / 8 GB`, no GPU, `$0` CPU charge during I/O wait, `5,000` concurrent sessions, `25 TPS` default) with deployment pattern `"harness"` (single-agent Strands/native). Routes Workload B (`session_duration == "over_8hr"`, `heavy_non_gpu`, `instance_type_requirement == "yes"`, `multi_agent == "yes"`, `crewai`) to `agentcore_compute_type = "instances"` (up to `14` days, Linux EC2 pricing + AgentCore management fee, immutable capacity provider) with deployment pattern `"framework_on_runtime"`.
expectations: Activates the agent-advisor skill
Routes Workload A to AgentCore `microvms` (`<= 8h`, `<= 2 vCPU / 8 GB`, `$0` CPU billing during I/O wait) + `harness`

Routes Workload B to AgentCore `instances` (up to `14` days, Linux EC2 + management fee, immutable capacity provider) + `framework_on_runtime` (due to `over_8hr` / `heavy_non_gpu` / `instance_type_requirement` and `multi_agent` / `crewai`)

evals.prompt: We are migrating our Python Temporal-orchestrated AI agents to AWS. Should we rewrite our `@workflow.defn` Temporal workflows into AWS Step Functions or AgentCore, migrate in-flight Temporal workflow histories directly across clusters, and host our Temporal Workers on AWS Lambda or AgentCore?
evals.expected_output: Explicitly forbids rewriting Temporal `@workflow.defn` workflow code into AWS Step Functions or AgentCore. Presents **Way 1: Temporal Cloud (default, ~$0.01/action ballpark)** vs **Way 2: Self-hosted Temporal Server (`EKS + Aurora/RDS`)**, notes there is **no cross-cluster live workflow history migration tool** (must use drain-and-cutover / versioned task queues), explains that Tier 1 continuous gRPC long-polling eliminates standard `lambda`, `agentcore`, and `lambda_microvms` (`ECS Fargate` is default for Temporal Workers), and notes that `<15m` activities on Way 1 can optionally use **Temporal Lambda Serverless Workers**, which MUST be labeled **`Public Preview`**.
expectations: Activates the agent-advisor skill

Explicitly states NEVER to rewrite Temporal Workflow code into Step Functions or AgentCore, compares Way 1 (Temporal Cloud default, `~$0.01/action`) vs Way 2 (Self-hosted on `EKS + Aurora/RDS`), and notes no cross-cluster live history migration tool exists (drain-and-cutover)

Explains that continuous polling eliminates standard `lambda`, `agentcore`, and `lambda_microvms` (defaulting Temporal Workers to `ECS Fargate`), while labeling `<15m + Way 1` Lambda Serverless Workers as **`Public Preview`**

evals.prompt: Score the 5 agent runtimes for migrating our Heroku web app to AWS: it has a React SPA, a stateless FastAPI CRUD API with Postgres, and a single synchronous `/summarize` route that calls `openai.chat.completions.create()` once with zero tool loops, zero memory, and zero autonomous agent sessions.
evals.expected_output: Identifies `0` `agent_session` units (a stateless CRUD app with a single non-agent LLM call is NOT an autonomous agent workload), declines forcing it through the 5-agent-runtime scoring funnel, and cleanly redirects web/infra migration to `heroku-to-aws` (or `gcp-to-aws` for GCP sources) and the synchronous OpenAI SDK call migration to `llm-to-bedrock` / `ai-to-bedrock`.
expectations: Activates the agent-advisor skill
Identifies `0` `agent_session` units (stateless CRUD + single synchronous LLM call is not an agent workload) and declines forcing an agent runtime recommendation
Cleanly redirects platform migration to `heroku-to-aws` and pure LLM SDK migration to `llm-to-bedrock` / `ai-to-bedrock`

evals.prompt: In our target AgentCore Gateway design, our security lead wants to use Gateway per-tenant rate limits (`0` RPS for restricted roles) as our primary authorization control instead of authoring Cedar policies. Audit this security assumption.
evals.expected_output: Rejects using AgentCore Gateway rate limits as an authorization/security control: **Gateway rate limits execute BEFORE Cedar Policy evaluation and are fail-open** — they are strictly a **cost and traffic-shaping control, NOT a security boundary**. Requires enforcing authorization via **AgentCore Policy Engine (Cedar)** (`default-deny`, `FORBID` always overrides `permit`) plus least-privilege IAM roles.
expectations: Activates the agent-advisor skill
Flags that AgentCore Gateway rate limits run BEFORE Cedar Policy and are **fail-open** (cost/traffic control only, never a security boundary)
Recommends enforcing tool authorization with Cedar policies (`FORBID` overrides `permit`, default-deny) and scoped IAM

evals.prompt: Audit four choices in a proposed AWS agent POC repo: (1) `aws_lambda_function_url` with `authorization_type = "NONE"`, (2) the ECS Fargate POC Terraform module creating a brand-new VPC, NAT Gateway, and ALB, (3) the EKS POC manifests provisioning a new EKS cluster and node IAM roles, and (4) Kubernetes `env` setting `TEMPORAL_TLS_CERT_PATH` via `valueFrom.secretKeyRef` to raw PEM bytes.
evals.expected_output: Flags all four POC guardrails: (1) `aws_lambda_function_url` MUST enforce **`authorization_type = "AWS_IAM"`** (never `"NONE"`); (2) ECS/Batch POC Terraform must accept existing `vpc_id`/`subnet_ids` and **never create VPC, NAT Gateway, or ALB**; (3) EKS POC manifests must deploy into an existing cluster/IRSA/Pod Identity and **never create an EKS cluster or IAM roles**; and (4) Temporal TLS certificates in Kubernetes MUST be **mounted as Secret volume files** (passing filesystem paths like `/etc/temporal/tls/tls.crt` to `*_PATH` env vars — injecting PEM content into `*_PATH` via `secretKeyRef` breaks file-path loading).
expectations: Activates the agent-advisor skill
Requires `authorization_type = "AWS_IAM"` on Lambda Function URLs (forbidding `"NONE"`) and forbids POC modules from creating new VPC/NAT/ALB (ECS/Batch) or new EKS clusters/IAM roles (EKS)
Fixes Temporal K8s TLS handling by mounting Secret volumes as files and pointing `*_PATH` env vars to the mounted file paths rather than `secretKeyRef` PEM strings

evals.prompt: Our Python LangGraph agent is already running reliably on Amazon ECS Fargate in production, and we do NOT want to migrate compute runtimes. We just want to add cross-session user memory, governed MCP tool discovery, and online trace evaluations. How should we approach this?
evals.expected_output: Uses the **`add_capabilities`** workflow rather than a compute migration: keeps the LangGraph agent running on **Amazon ECS Fargate** (`compute` unchanged) and attaches modular **Bedrock AgentCore** building blocks independently over AWS SDK/HTTPS — **AgentCore Memory** (short-term events + long-term semantic/user-preference extraction), **AgentCore Gateway** (governed MCP tool registry + Cedar Policy), and **AgentCore Observability / Evaluations** (OTLP trace export + online evaluators).
expectations: Activates the agent-advisor skill
Selects the `add_capabilities` pattern keeping existing ECS Fargate compute untouched rather than forcing a runtime migration to AgentCore Runtime
Maps the three requested capabilities cleanly to modular AgentCore Memory, AgentCore Gateway (+ Policy), and AgentCore Evaluations / Observability

evals.prompt: Check AWS pricing references via MCP and compare the compute billing model for `100,000` interactive `5-minute` (`300s`) agent sessions per month (`1 vCPU / 2 GB`) where each session spends `85%` of wall-clock time (`255s`) idle waiting on Bedrock streaming and external APIs: **AgentCore MicroVMs** vs **ECS Fargate**.
evals.expected_output: Queries `awspricing` / `awsknowledge` MCP tools without raw CLI calls and contrasts the two billing models: **AgentCore MicroVMs** charge **`$0` for CPU during I/O wait** (billing active CPU-seconds for only the `15%` = `45s` active compute per session, plus peak memory GB-seconds across the session), whereas **ECS Fargate** bills full wall-clock vCPU-seconds and GB-seconds for the entire `300s` (or idle warm pool time between sessions), making AgentCore MicroVMs substantially cheaper for spiky, I/O-wait-dominated interactive agent sessions (excluding identical Bedrock token spend).
expectations: Activates the agent-advisor skill and uses connected MCP tools (`awspricing` / `awsknowledge`) without raw `aws` CLI commands

Accurately contrasts AgentCore MicroVMs (`$0` CPU billing during the `85%` / `255s` I/O wait; billed only on active `45s` CPU-seconds + peak memory GB-seconds) against ECS Fargate (billed for full `300s` wall-clock vCPU + memory plus any idle task capacity)
Notes that Bedrock model token costs apply separately to both runtimes

evals.prompt: Verify via AWS documentation how AWS Lambda Managed Instances (`lambda_microvms`) differ from standard AWS Lambda execution environments for concurrent I/O-bound requests, and confirm how model-availability verification should behave when operating in a strict read-only assessment environment.
evals.expected_output: Uses `awsknowledge` MCP tools to explain AWS Lambda Managed Instances (`lambda_microvms` — customer EC2 capacity managed by Lambda supporting multi-concurrency per execution environment and predictable steady-state economics, while still subject to Lambda invocation timeout limits verified via live docs), and confirms that in strict read-only mode live inference probes (`Converse` / `InvokeModel` / `verify_model_path.py` data-plane calls) must NOT be executed — use control-plane read-only APIs (`ListFoundationModels`, `ListInferenceProfiles`, `GetFoundationModelAvailability`) or mark runtime/model verifications `provisional`.
expectations: Activates the agent-advisor skill and consults `awsknowledge` MCP tools without running raw `aws` CLI commands
Explains how Lambda Managed Instances (`lambda_microvms`) differ from standard Lambda (multi-concurrency on managed EC2 instances vs single-request isolation, plus timeout constraints)
Enforces skipping data-plane `Converse`/`InvokeModel` probes in read-only mode in favor of control-plane read-only checks or `provisional` status
